after: ## How do private and public sector enterprises differ? (2.1.1)
alt: Two columns. The private sector is owned by individuals, partners, members or shareholders, usually aims for profit and includes sole traders, partnerships, cooperatives and private and public limited companies. The public sector is owned by the government, usually aims to provide a service and includes public corporations.
caption: Who owns the enterprise decides its sector; a public limited company is still in the private sector.

after: ## What are the features of each type of private sector enterprise? (2.1.2)
alt: Five rows comparing sole trader, partnership, cooperative, private limited company and public limited company by owners, how capital and profits are handled, and liability. Sole traders and ordinary partners have unlimited liability, cooperative members have one vote each, and shareholders in both kinds of limited company have limited liability.
caption: Liability changes from unlimited to limited once the business becomes a company with shareholders.

after: ## What are public corporations and why do they exist? (2.1.2)
alt: A central box describes a public corporation: owned by the government, run by a board it appoints and reporting to a minister. Five reasons point into it: essential services, avoiding wasteful duplication, loss-making areas, strategic or security reasons, and protecting jobs.
caption: Public corporations exist to serve the public where profit alone would not.

after: ## Which type of ownership suits which situation? (2.1.2)
alt: Five situations each lead to a suitable form of ownership: a lone plumber to a sole trader, two architects to a partnership, fifty fishermen to a cooperative, a growing family bakery to a private limited company, and an airline needing large sums to a public limited company.
caption: Choose the form whose capital, control and liability fit the scenario, and give the reason.

alt: Headquarters in the home country links to factories and outlets in host countries, with profits possibly flowing back home. Five reasons for MNCs are listed, then four positive and four negative impacts on a host country.
caption: An MNC brings jobs and investment to a host country but may send profits home and push out local firms.

alt: The franchisor gives the franchisee its brand, products or recipes, training and advertising; the franchisee pays an initial fee and a royalty. A grid sets out the advantages and disadvantages for the franchisee and for the franchisor.
caption: Always say whether an advantage belongs to the franchisor or the franchisee.

after: ## How do enterprises choose a location? (2.1.5)
alt: Three businesses rank location factors differently. A cement works puts raw materials and transport first, a hair salon puts markets and competition first, and an online clothing retailer puts warehousing, logistics and wi-fi first.
caption: The right location factors depend on what the business does and how it reaches customers.
